carousels.name: 3 p*rn habits researchers link to addiction

slides.title: 3 p*rn habits researchers link to [[p*rn addiction.]]
slides.sub: If you do #2, you'll recognize yourself instantly.

slides.title: [[Binge]] sessions
slides.body:
Not a few minutes — hours of p*rn in one sitting, often late at night.

Researchers studying problematic p*rn use see this pattern again and again.

slides.title: Tab [[jumping]]
slides.body: Ten tabs open. Never finishing one video before searching for the next. That endless hunt for something newer is a key marker of compulsive p*rn use.

slides.title: Needing [[more]]
slides.body: More time, more videos, more intense p*rn to feel the same thing. A 2025 study of over 2,000 men linked this kind of tolerance to losing control over p*rn use.

slides.title: Recognize [[yourself?]]
slides.body: These patterns don't make you broken. They're signals that p*rn has more control than you'd like. Signals can be acted on.
slides.note: Which of the 3 do you see in yourself? Comment the number 👇

Spot the pattern.

carousels.name: A p*rn relapse starts days before the screen

slides.title: Your p*rn relapse started [[3 days before]] you opened the tab.
slides.sub: The warning signs nobody notices — until it's too late.

slides.title: It starts with [[feelings]]
slides.body: Stress builds. You feel lonely, irritable or flat. Addiction clinics describe this emotional stage as what often comes before a p*rn relapse.

slides.title: Then the [[thinking]] changes
slides.body: "I've been good, I deserve a break." "Just a quick look won't hurt." Your brain starts making the case for p*rn.

slides.title: Then the [[guard]] drops
slides.body: Phone back in bed. Blocker "just for a minute" off. Skipping check-ins. By the time you open p*rn, the relapse is already halfway done.

slides.title: Stop it [[early]]
items: Catch the "I deserve it" thoughts about p*rn.
Never loosen guardrails on a bad week.
Tell someone before it gets to the screen.
slides.note: What's YOUR early warning sign? Share it below 👇

slides.title:
Catch the p*rn relapse
[[before it starts.]]
slides.lead: Daily journaling to spot your patterns, check-ins with real people and a panic button for the urge.

carousels.name: The 6 PM p*rn trigger: coming home

slides.title: You walk in the door. Bag down. [[P*rn urge on.]]
slides.sub: Why getting home is one of the riskiest moments of the day.

slides.title: The [[switch-off]] moment
slides.body: All day you hold it together. The second you're home, the pressure drops. For many people, that's exactly when the p*rn urge shows up.

slides.title: Empty room, [[empty]] evening
slides.body: Nobody around, nothing planned, phone in your hand. P*rn becomes the default way to "decompress" after work.

slides.title: Build a new [[ritual]]
slides.body: Your brain needs a different signal that the day is over. Replace the p*rn ritual with one you choose — before you even sit down.

slides.title: Your [[coming-home]] routine
items: Change clothes the moment you walk in.
Shower or work out before touching your phone.
Leave the phone charging by the door for 30 minutes.
Plan the evening on your way home.
slides.note: When does your p*rn urge hit hardest? Comment the time 👇

slides.title:
Come home to yourself,
[[not to p*rn.]]
slides.lead: Daily actions, a p*rn blocker for your evenings and streaks that grow every night you stay clean.

carousels.name: Is p*rn addiction real? What science says

slides.title: "P*rn addiction isn't real." [[Here's what science actually says.]]
slides.sub: And why the label matters less than you think.

slides.title: It's [[officially]] recognized
slides.body: The WHO's ICD-11 includes compulsive sexual behaviour disorder — and compulsive p*rn use is one of the ways it shows up.

slides.title: The [[debate]] is about the word
slides.body: Researchers still argue whether to call it "p*rn addiction" or "problematic p*rn use." What they agree on: loss of control is real for many people.

slides.title: You don't need a [[label]]
slides.body: If p*rn takes time, energy or confidence you want back, that's reason enough. You don't need a diagnosis to decide to stop.

slides.title: Ask yourself [[honestly]]
items: Have I tried to quit p*rn and failed?
Do I watch more p*rn than I planned?
Does p*rn affect my mood, sleep or relationships?
Do I hide it from people close to me?
slides.note: Do you think p*rn addiction is real? Tell us why 👇

slides.title:
Real or not —
[[you can quit p*rn.]]
slides.lead: Science-informed tools and guided lessons about p*rn addiction, built for shame-free progress.

carousels.name: P*rn for anxiety: the relief that makes it worse

slides.kicker: If you use it to calm down
slides.title: You watch p*rn to calm your anxiety. [[It's making it worse.]]
slides.sub: The relief loop that keeps so many people stuck.

slides.title: Quick [[relief]]
slides.body: Anxious, overwhelmed, can't switch off — p*rn gives a few minutes of escape. That relief is real. That's why it's so hard to stop.

slides.title: Then the [[crash]]
slides.body: Guilt, shame, wasted time — and the original worry is still there. Many people say they feel more anxious after p*rn, not less.

slides.title: The anxiety–p*rn [[loop]]
slides.body: P*rn doesn't fix the anxiety. It feeds it.

slides.title: Calm down [[without]] p*rn
items: Talk to someone — or a professional if it's constant.
